\chapter{Dog and Cat}
\label{ch:la-dog-and-cat}
\hlchaptermodality{17}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a dog and a cat in Latin, and say which of its two cat-words came first.}

Name canis, fēlēs, and cattus, then say which cat-word is Classical Latin's own and where the newcomer arrived from.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[canis, fēlēs, cattus]{canis, fēlēs, cattus — the expected word, and the word that pushed it out}

\label{lesson:LA-C17-canis-feles-cattus}



\begin{quote}
Spanish's \emph{perro} mysteriously displaced the word Latin gave it. Here is that word, and a parallel story about \textquotedblleft{}cat.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{canis} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{dog}\textquotedblright{}) is the direct source of English \textbf{canine}, French \textbf{chien}, Italian \textbf{cane} — and it's also the Latin word Spanish \textbf{inherited} first, as \textbf{can}. But Spanish's everyday word for dog is \emph{perro} instead, a word with \textbf{no confirmed etymology at all} — \emph{can} survives only in archaic or literary use, quietly pushed aside by a newcomer nobody can fully explain.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fēlēs and cattus — a similar displacement, this time INSIDE Latin}
Here is a parallel that happened \textbf{within Latin itself}, before any Romance language existed:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{fēlēs} was Classical Latin's own, original word for \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{cat}\textquotedblright{} — used by Cicero, Pliny, and others, and still preserved today in the scientific name for the domestic cat, \emph{\textbf{Felis catus}}.
  \item \textbf{cattus} (also \emph{catta}) is a \textbf{later} word that entered Latin as domestic cats themselves spread along Roman trade routes, out of their point of domestication in \textbf{Egypt} (c. 2000 BCE). \emph{Cattus} is most likely ultimately an \textbf{Afro-Asiatic} word (compare Nubian \emph{kadis}, \textquotedblleft{}cat\textquotedblright{}) — the word traveled \textbf{with the animal}.
\end{itemize}

By around 700 CE, \emph{cattus} had pushed \emph{fēlēs} out of everyday use almost everywhere — it's \emph{cattus}, not \emph{fēlēs}, that gives Spanish \emph{gato}, Italian \emph{gatto}, French \emph{chat}, and more.

\begin{culture}
Both \textquotedblleft{}dog\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}cat\textquotedblright{} show a Latin-inherited word getting pushed aside by a newcomer — but the two stories aren't equally well understood. \emph{Cattus} replacing \emph{fēlēs} is a well-documented, well-sourced piece of history, with a real trade-route explanation. \emph{Perro} replacing \emph{canis}-derived \emph{can} is genuinely \textbf{unexplained} — a real gap in the historical record, not just a simplification for beginners.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}canis\textquotedblright{} — dog, source of English \textquotedblleft{}canine\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}fēlēs\textquotedblright{} — Classical Latin's own word for cat
  \item \textquotedblleft{}cattus\textquotedblright{} — the newcomer that replaced it, probably from Egypt via Africa
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item What English word is a direct cousin of \textbf{canis}? (\textbf{Canine}.)
  \item Which Latin word for \textquotedblleft{}cat\textquotedblright{} is older? (\textbf{Fēlēs} — Classical Latin's own word, later displaced by \emph{cattus}.)
  \item Where does \emph{cattus} most likely come from? (An \textbf{Afro-Asiatic} word, probably from \textbf{Egypt}, that traveled with the cat itself.)
  \item Are the two displacements equally well understood? (\textbf{No} — \emph{cattus} has a sourced history; Spanish \emph{perro} remains a genuine mystery.)
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
